title: Who protects the unprotected?
hook: Some people can't be vaccinated. Can everyone else's immunity shield them?

knows: infections pass from person to person
vaccines or past infection can make a person immune

misconception: Immunity only protects the person who has it, so an outbreak will still reach most unprotected people; protection grows gradually with each extra immune person rather than tipping at a threshold.
objective: The learner can explain that each case's onward infections are R0 times the unprotected share, that once this falls below 1 chains of infection shrink and die out, and that in a simple well-mixed model this happens when more than 1 - 1/R0 are immune (75% when R0 = 4), which also shields people who are not immune.

claims.text: R0 is the average number of people one case infects in a population where nobody is immune.
claims.source: Anderson & May (1991), Infectious Diseases of Humans: Dynamics and Control, Oxford University Press, ch. 2; Fine, Eames & Heymann (2011), 'Herd immunity: a rough guide', Clinical Infectious Diseases 52(7): 911-916.

claims.text: In a simple model where everyone mixes with everyone at random and immunity fully blocks catching and passing on the disease, a case infects on average R0 x (1 - p) people when a share p is immune.
claims.source: Anderson & May (1991), ch. 5; Fine, Eames & Heymann (2011), Clin Infect Dis 52(7): 911-916.

claims.text: In that model, once more than 1 - 1/R0 of people are immune, each case causes fewer than one new case on average, so chains of infection tend to shrink and die out; for R0 = 4 the threshold is 75%.
claims.source: R0(1 - p) < 1 iff p > 1 - 1/R0; with R0 = 4, 1 - 1/4 = 0.75. Anderson & May (1991); Fine, Eames & Heymann (2011).

claims.text: In the stage model (400 people, each case contacts 4 random townspeople), one case among a town that is 80% immune infects on average about 4 of the 80 unprotected people, counting the first case; at 50% immune it is about 146 of 200.
claims.source: Demo.tsx: 200 seeded runs per setting (mean 4.2 of 80 at 80%; 145.9 of 200 at 50%). The stage shows its own 200-run average for whatever share the learner picks.

claims.text: Below the threshold an outbreak can still die out early by chance, but when it takes off it reaches a large share of the unprotected.
claims.source: Branching-process extinction probability; Diekmann, Heesterbeek & Britton (2013), Mathematical Tools for Understanding Infectious Disease Dynamics, Princeton University Press, ch. 1 and 3.

claims.text: Real populations are not well mixed: when unprotected people cluster together, outbreaks can spread among them even when the overall immune share is above the simple threshold.
claims.source: Fine, Eames & Heymann (2011), Clin Infect Dis 52(7): 911-916; Salathe & Bonhoeffer (2008), 'The effect of opinion clustering on disease outbreaks', Journal of the Royal Society Interface 5(29): 1505-1508.

claims.text: Some people cannot be vaccinated against a given disease, for example babies too young for that vaccine or some people with weakened immune systems.
claims.source: CDC, General Best Practice Guidelines for Immunization: Contraindications and Precautions; Fine, Eames & Heymann (2011).

claims.text: The disease on the stage is made up, with R0 = 4; real vaccines are not perfect, which this model ignores.
claims.source: Modelling choice stated on the stage and in the reveal.

recall.question: A disease has R0 = 5 in a simple well-mixed model. Roughly what share must be immune for outbreaks to die out?
recall.why: Each case infects 5 x (unprotected share). That drops below 1 when fewer than 1 in 5 are unprotected, so more than 1 - 1/5 = 80% must be immune.
